title: Trump Just Cut Off Trade With a NATO Ally Over Iran. India's $200 Billion Relationship With the US Is Taking Notes.
excerpt: Spain refused to back the Iran war and got a public trade embargo threat at the Ankara summit. India, which protested US strikes that killed its sailors, faces the same logic at five times the economic scale.
body:
Donald Trump just showed the world what happens when an ally refuses to fall in line on the Iran war. India, which has publicly protested American strikes that killed its sailors, should be paying close attention.

At the NATO summit in Ankara on Wednesday, Trump ordered Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to immediately halt all trade with Spain — a fellow NATO member — calling the country "a terrible partner" and "a wasted cause." The reason: Spain refused to let the United States use its airspace or military bases for operations against Iran, and it was the only NATO member to reject the alliance's new 5 per cent GDP defence spending target. This move, while targeting a NATO ally, sends a clear message about the potential for economic leverage in international relations, a message that resonates with India's own complex geopolitical balancing act.

"Cut off all trade with Spain, please, including visits," Trump told Bessent, with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte sitting beside him. "Let's see how hostile they remain when they call up, and they say 'please, please, we want to trade with you, sir.'" This public declaration, reported by outlets like Reuters, highlighted the President's willingness to use economic pressure as a tool of foreign policy.

It was the second time Trump has threatened a total trade embargo on Spain. In March, he made a similar declaration, though trade continued normally. However, the International Emergency Economic Powers Act gives a US president sweeping powers to restrict commerce with any country — the same statute used to sanction Iran, Russia and North Korea. Legal experts suggest Trump could invoke it against Spain, though it would almost certainly face court challenges. As of now, the trade cutoff remains a threat, not a fully implemented policy, but the public declaration itself carries significant weight.

## Why India Cannot Look Away

India is not in NATO and has no defence spending commitment to the alliance. Yet, the dynamics that just put Spain in Trump's crosshairs are uncomfortably familiar for New Delhi. The spectacle of a major US ally facing such a public threat from Washington underscores the potential for economic pressure, a scenario that Indian policymakers are keenly aware of given their own strategic autonomy. For the Indian diaspora, particularly those with business ties or professional interests in both countries, such actions highlight the volatility that can impact global trade and investment flows.

Consider the situation with Iran. India has been walking a tightrope over the Strait of Hormuz crisis, which has intensified all week. On one side, Washington is India's most important strategic partner — the two countries are on the verge of what officials have called a "very, very close" bilateral trade deal, and defence cooperation has never been deeper. On the other side, American strikes on commercial vessels in the Gulf have killed three Indian mariners, injured others, and endangered thousands of Indian seafarers who crew ships transiting the world's most volatile waterway.

India's response has been pointed. External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar personally called US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to register "India's strong protest" over the strikes that killed the three sailors on the tanker MT Settebello. The Ministry of External Affairs summoned US Chargé d'Affaires Jason Meeks — not once, but twice — to demand that the attacks on commercial shipping stop. "Such lethal actions against commercial shipping are not justified," Jaishankar said publicly, a statement reported by Indian media outlets like The Hindu. This firm stance underscores India's commitment to protecting its citizens and commercial interests, even when it means challenging a key ally.

That is, by the standards of Indian diplomacy, remarkably blunt language directed at a strategic partner. This firm stance underscores India's commitment to protecting its citizens and commercial interests, even when it means challenging a key ally.

## The Trade Dimension

Now layer in Trump's proven willingness to use trade as a weapon of compliance. Spain's bilateral trade with the United States is roughly $40 billion a year. India's is more than five times that — over $200 billion and climbing. The economic consequences of even a partial disruption would be staggering for both nations.

The trade deal that American and Indian officials have been negotiating for months sits at a delicate moment. At the recent US-India Strategic and Partnership Forum (USISPF) Summit, the Indian ambassador to the US, Taranjit Singh Sandhu, stated that an agreement was "very, very close." However, India has also drawn a red line: it will not accept terms less favourable than those given to Pakistan under the new US-Pakistan trade framework. That kind of conditionality does not play well with a president who just called a NATO ally a "wasted cause" for setting its own terms.

Indian IT services companies — TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCLTech — generate a significant share of their revenue from American clients. Hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals on H-1B visas work across the United States. Indian pharmaceutical exports to the US were worth $8.7 billion last year, according to data from the Ministry of Commerce and Industry. None of these flows would survive a Trump-style embargo, however unlikely one remains. For NRIs, particularly those in the tech and healthcare sectors, any disruption to this trade relationship could directly impact job security, business opportunities, and the flow of remittances back home, affecting their financial stability and ability to support families in India.

## The NATO Precedent

The Ankara summit was supposed to be a show of unity. Instead, it produced $80 billion in military aid pledges for Ukraine, a commitment to 5 per cent GDP defence spending by 2035, and the spectacle of the alliance's most powerful member publicly humiliating a founding partner over its refusal to support a war that most of its citizens oppose. The connection to India lies in the demonstration of unilateral economic power, even against an ally, which could set a precedent for how the US approaches other strategic partners. This could particularly impact India's efforts to diversify its trade relationships and maintain strategic autonomy, a key concern for its economic and geopolitical stability.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez played the moment coolly, telling reporters he had a "very cordial" conversation with Trump during the summit. Behind closed doors, sources indicated Trump struck a different tone, telling allies he wanted to remain in NATO and claiming there was "love" and "a lot of unity" at the gathering. French President Emmanuel Macron said he did not hear any complaints from Trump in the private sessions.

But the public message landed. And for India, it crystallised a risk that has been building since the Hormuz crisis began: Trump's willingness to use economic coercion extends far beyond traditional adversaries. If a NATO ally with a 2 per cent GDP defence contribution can be threatened with a full trade cutoff, the threshold for punishing a non-aligned partner is lower than New Delhi may have assumed. This precedent could influence how Indian policymakers approach future negotiations and strategic alignments, potentially impacting the ease of doing business for Indian companies and professionals abroad.

## What the Diaspora Is Watching

For the 4.4 million Indian Americans — the wealthiest immigrant group in the United States, deeply embedded in tech, medicine, finance and law — the Spain episode is a stress test for the bilateral relationship they depend on. Every trade disruption, every diplomatic slight, ripples through visa processing, business investment and community standing. The stability of US-India relations is crucial for many NRIs, impacting everything from professional opportunities to the ease of travel and maintaining family ties. Any perceived instability could also affect their ability to invest in India or facilitate family visits, which are vital for maintaining cultural connections.

The irony is that India has been more accommodating of American interests in the Middle East than almost any other major economy. It has shifted energy purchases, moderated its Iran relationship and quietly supported freedom of navigation. Its protests have been narrowly focused on the safety of its citizens, not on opposing the war itself.

But if Spain's offence was refusing to lend airspace, India's offence could one day be refusing to cut off Iranian oil entirely, or demanding better trade terms, or simply being too independent for a president who views every relationship as a scorecard.

The uranium deal with Australia that Modi signed hours earlier in Melbourne tells one side of the story: India is diversifying its partnerships, building resilience, reducing dependency on any single power. The scene from Ankara tells the other: in Trump's world, there are allies and there are targets. The line between them has never been thinner.
